lesson.title: Whole Numbers, No Rounding: The int Type
lesson.summary: The int type stores whole numbers with no fractional part and, unlike in many other languages, Python integers can grow to arbitrary size without overflowing.
lesson.body:
An integer, written as int in Python, represents a whole number with no fractional part: values like 0, 42, -17, or 1000000. Integers are the type you reach for whenever a quantity is inherently countable rather than measured, such as the number of students in a class, the index of an item in a list, or the number of times a loop has run. Because they carry no decimal component, integers can be compared and combined without the rounding surprises that come up with decimal values, which the next lesson on the float type covers in detail.

One feature that distinguishes Python's integers from those in many other languages is that they have no fixed size limit. In a language like C or Java, an int is typically stored in a fixed number of bits, commonly 32, which caps the largest representable value and causes overflow if you exceed it. Python integers grow automatically to hold however many digits are needed, limited only by available memory. You can compute something like 2 ** 200 and get back an exact 61 digit integer, with no loss of precision and no special handling required from you.

Literals of type int can be written directly in code: x = 7, y = -3, z = 0. Python also lets you use underscores to make long numbers easier to read, so population = 1_400_000_000 is exactly the same value as 1400000000, just easier for a human to parse at a glance. This does not change the type or the value in any way; it is purely a readability feature for whoever is writing or reading the code.

Here is a small trace to make the behavior concrete:

count = 10
count = count + 5
count = count * 2
print(count)

Start with count bound to the integer 10. Adding 5 produces a new integer 15, and count is rebound to it. Multiplying by 2 produces 30, and count is rebound again. The final print shows 30, and at every step the type of count stayed int, because adding or multiplying two integers in Python always produces another integer; division is the one arithmetic operator that can hand you back a float instead, which the arithmetic operators lesson explains later in this unit. Recognizing when a value should be an integer, rather than a float pretending to be whole, is what allows later lessons on integer division and the modulo operator to make sense, since both operators lean specifically on the fact that integers have no fractional part.

Integers can also be written in bases other than base ten, which becomes useful once you start working closer to how a computer actually stores data. Prefixing digits with 0b writes a value in binary, 0o writes it in octal, and 0x writes it in hexadecimal, so 0b1010, 0o12, and 0xA are three different ways of writing the same integer, 10. Python converts all of them to the same ordinary int as soon as the code runs; print(0xA) displays 10, not "0xA", because the base used in the literal is only a detail of how you typed the number, not something the integer itself remembers afterward.
